extracted.intended_audience: media professionals, editors, newsletter creators, and readers interested in curated news briefings
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or describing the qualities of a daily curated email news briefing (like the Quartz Daily Brief), focusing on curation, tone, structure, format, timeliness, and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curated obsessions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Curated obsessions? How can anyone be against that?” — the briefing selects a set of focused topics or 'obsessions' to highlight each edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author appreciates newsletters that theme or obsess over particular subjects; curation around a few recurrent obsessions gives texture to a reader's news day and makes the product distinctive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑tempos for storytelling / curated edition timing
rubrics_metrics.description: In the era of the two‑tempos for storytelling, the curated edition 'stops you at a specific time each day to remind you of what you should and must know right that minute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful daily brief establishes a regular tempo — a fixed delivery moment that captures the reader's attention and provides a concise roundup relevant at that specific time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: chatty and personalized voice
rubrics_metrics.description: “This briefing is chatty… I get the feeling Quartz is writing to me and me only.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conversational, intimate tone that reads as if directed to a single reader can increase engagement and make the briefing feel bespoke rather than generic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format: plain text, no visuals, concise
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are also no visuals. This is just plain text. Quick, to the point…"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimalist formatting and succinct copy can be effective — plain text emphasizes speed and readability and may help the briefing feel fast and portable; however, it forgoes visual indexing or imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines that summarize main stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The briefing includes a headline summary of the main stories: e.g., 'Quartz Weekend Brief—Twitter jihad, mobile finance, disrupting disruption, “smart dumb”'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, concise headline summaries help readers quickly grasp the major items covered and decide what to read in depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of internal headlines/indexing can be a feature
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are also no headlines to hep me index. Which may be a good thing…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not having section headlines can make the piece feel more like a direct note to the reader; lack of rigid indexing may enhance the conversational feel, though it reduces scannability for some users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed provenance curation: internal and external picks
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections like 'Five things on Quartz we especially liked' and 'Five things elsewhere that made us smarter' show a mix of in‑house and external selections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing internally produced content with links or mentions of notable external pieces broadens value to readers and signals editorial judgment rather than pure self‑promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named structural segments (Obsession interlude, Matters of debate, Surprising discoveries)
rubrics_metrics.description: The brief uses recurring segment labels such as 'Quartz obsession interlude', 'Matters of debate', and 'Surprising discoveries' to organize content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct recurring segments give readers predictable structure and variety — e.g., opinion/debate, quirky finds, deep dives — which helps set expectations and maintain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content selection: provocative and interesting items
rubrics_metrics.description: “In typical Quartz style: provocatively interesting.” Items chosen are attention‑grabbing or thought‑provoking (e.g., 'If Facebook was a country, it would be a dictatorship').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing provocative hooks or counterintuitive findings increases shareability and reader curiosity; selections should still be defensible and relevant to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising or curiosity‑driven discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: The brief highlights surprising facts or discoveries (e.g., '99% of the plastic in our oceans is missing. Sea creatures may be eating it').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including startling or novel facts yields emotional engagement and helps the brief stand out among routine summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of short illustrative examples or anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Short anecdotes or excerpts (e.g., the auction paddle example) are used to illustrate a story's flavor quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief illustrative details can make summaries more vivid and memorable without requiring deep reporting inside the email itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and relevance (news that 'grabbed' the author)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author lists 'headlines that grabbed me in today's Quartz Brief' and emphasizes topical items (e.g., euro zone, UK, Iraq events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good daily brief prioritizes immediacy and items of current relevance that justify inclusion in a limited format rather than generic evergreen content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement / call to action
rubrics_metrics.description: The brief closes with an explicit invitation: 'Please send any news, comments, disruptive ideas, and dumb ideas to hi@qz.com. You can follow us on Twitter…'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active invitations for reader submissions, feedback, and social follow‑ups foster community, surface tips, and increase loyalty; calls to action should be simple and clearly placed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of seriousness and playfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The mix of serious geopolitical items with lighter pieces (IUD perception problem, military dolphins, domain auctions) shows a balance of weight and whimsy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining hard news with quirky or lighter items keeps the brief engaging across moods and broadens appeal while demonstrating editorial range.
